title: Practice: how greedy, ε-greedy and UCB choose
note: Three problems (2026-11-05, after two pilot sessions where both learners missed the test's lucky-start greedy items, T1 and V11): P7 (greedy after a lucky start: the favourite's average falls with a poor day and greedy switches; needs greedy's own rule, n05.f1, which no problem needed before, so a learner who taught "greedy sticks with the trial winner" sees Kai go wrong), P3 (greedy against UCB after an unlucky start) and P2 (what one pick does to every score). Each problem has a caveat, a nuance learners rarely put into words: when Kai would otherwise solve every problem, it reads the first one its notes leave open the plausible wrong way (never against the notes). P4 (audio tours) and the ε-greedy problems are in stash/practice.json. Two rounds of three problems, from the team's item design (P1 to P6). Round 2 repeats round 1's facts in new settings (P4 repeats P2's, P5 P1's and adds UCB, P6 P3's over many rounds), so a correction in round 1 can carry over. Options state only the prediction. Answers and worked solutions stay on the server and are shown on the results page after the final test. Each solution step lists the facts it relies on. `needs` lists the teachable facts without which the answer can't be reached, in the order the steps use them: in the recursive condition Kai can only be right when its notebook holds all of them, correctly explained. Given facts (the setup, averages, trying each option once) are never needed: Kai knows them and the stems repeat them. `beliefs` give, for each needed fact, the answer Kai's assumption for that fact leads to (the fact's `assume` in the graph, word for word; `when: vague` for how Kai reads a vague explanation, where that differs). When needed facts are missing, Kai reasons from the assumption of the first one in `needs` order whose assumption leads somewhere wrong, says that it is guessing, and its wrong answer follows from its own steps. Every wrong option is the prediction of a named misconception (Kai's or a known learner one), so no option can be ruled out without the facts.

beliefs.belief: Greedy settles on whichever option leads after the first tries and sticks with it for good, without ever switching.

items.title: Ice-cream flavours
items.prompt: A café features one of three ice-cream flavours each day, chosen with greedy, and scores each day's sales out of 10. The true averages, unknown to the café, are A 8, B 6 and C 5, and most days score within 1 point of their flavour's true average. On the three trial days A scores 7.5, B has an unusually good day and scores 9, and C scores 5. On day 4 greedy features B, which scores 5. Which flavour does greedy feature on day 5, and on most days after that?
options: B on day 5 and after: it won the trials
A on day 5, and mostly A after that
A on day 5, then back to B
C, the one with the least promising start

steps.text: Greedy features the flavour with the highest average so far, and updates the average of the one it features.
After day 4, B's average is (9 + 5) / 2 = 7, below A's 7.5, so on day 5 greedy switches to A.
A's days score around 8, so A's average stays above B's 7, which no longer changes because B isn't featured: mostly A after that.

caveat.about: Greedy updates only the average of the option it features; the others' averages stay exactly as they were until they are featured again.
caveat.misreading: While A is featured, B's average keeps drifting back towards B's usual days, so after a while B's average climbs above A's again and greedy goes back to B.

items.title: Two cakes
items.prompt: Two cafés test the same two new cakes and score each day's sales out of 10. Cake A is truly better: its days usually score between 7 and 9. Cake B's days always score between 5 and 7. On the first two days both cafés try each cake once; in both, A has an unusually bad day (3) and B scores 6. From then on café 1 uses greedy and café 2 uses UCB. Which café ends up selling mostly cake A?

steps.text: After the first two days, A's average is 3 and B's is 6.
Greedy picks B. B's days score 5 to 7, so B's average stays above 3, greedy never picks A again, and A's average stays at 3.
UCB adds a bonus. Each day B is picked, B's bonus shrinks.
Each day A is not picked, A's bonus grows.
So A's score eventually passes B's, UCB tries A again, A's average rises towards 8, and UCB then mostly sells A.

beliefs.belief: If greedy keeps going, the averages correct themselves over time, so greedy finds the best option in the end.
Every bonus shrinks as rounds pass, whether its option is picked or not.
An option's bonus stays the same while it is not picked.
The bonus of an option that is not picked grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals.
UCB picks the option it is least sure about, the one tried the fewest times, whatever its average.

caveat.about: Cake B's days never score below 5, so its average can never fall to A's 3: once A is behind, greedy never picks it again.
caveat.misreading: Sooner or later B will have a run of bad days that pulls its average below A's 3, and then greedy goes back to A and finds out A is better, so café 1 ends up mostly on A too.

items.title: Exercise types
items.prompt: A language app picks the next exercise type with UCB. Before this round: Flashcards average 6.3, bonus 1.0 (tried 20 times); Dialogues average 5.0, bonus 2.5 (tried 3 times); Listening average 4.0, bonus 1.5 (tried 8 times). UCB picks Dialogues, and the learner scores exactly 5.0 on it. What happens to the three scores (average plus bonus) for the next round?
options: Dialogues' score falls; the other two rise slightly
Dialogues' score falls; the other two stay the same
All three scores stay the same

steps.text: The scores were Flashcards 7.3, Dialogues 7.5 and Listening 5.5, so UCB picked Dialogues.
The new result equals Dialogues' average, so the average stays 5.0.
Dialogues was tried once more, so its bonus shrinks and its score falls.
Flashcards and Listening were not picked, so their bonuses grow slightly with the round number.

beliefs.belief: Every bonus shrinks as rounds pass, whether its option is picked or not.
An option's bonus stays the same while it is not picked.
The bonus of an option that is not picked grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals.

caveat.about: Every round that passes makes the bonus of each option that isn't picked grow a little, even after a single round.
caveat.misreading: My notes say a bonus grows when its option isn't picked for a long time; Flashcards and Listening were only left out for this one round, which isn't long, so their bonuses stay as they were.
